India’s digital economy is entering a new phase. AI adoption, cloud-led enterprise transformation and rising digital consumption are driving an extraordinary build-out of data centre infrastructure, with India expected to become the second-largest data centre market in Asia-Pacific.  
But building data centres is only part of the challenge. Powering them is another. 
Electricity demand from the sector is set to rise dramatically over the coming years. For large-load consumers, that raises fundamental questions around where capacity can be built, how reliable power can be secured and which procurement models can deliver the right balance of cost, resilience and sustainability. 
Our recent report, ‘India’s data centre landscape: powering the digital economy’, explores the rapidly evolving market and the energy challenges that could shape its next phase of growth. 
Which markets offer the strongest opportunities? How are leading operators approaching power procurement? And could constraints around grids, renewables and water slow India’s data centre ambitions? 
Fill in the form on this page to access the report and explore our analysis. Or, read on for a short introduction:  
Can India’s power system support the data centre boom? 
Data centres are becoming a significant new source of electricity demand in India. As facilities become larger and AI workloads more energy intensive, securing sufficient power is becoming a central consideration in investment and site selection. 
The challenge is not simply procuring enough electricity. Mission-critical facilities require reliable, scalable supply, while hyperscalers and other major technology companies are simultaneously pursuing ambitious clean energy targets. Traditional grid supply can therefore struggle to meet operators’ requirements around reliability, sustainability and long-term cost certainty.  
What could rapidly rising data centre demand mean for India’s wider power market? And where could grid connectivity and infrastructure become barriers to expansion? 
Fill out the form on this page to explore Wood Mackenzie’s outlook for data centre power demand and the implications for large-load consumers. 
How will data centres procure their power?
The growth of data centres is already helping reshape corporate power procurement in India. 
Captive and group captive generation, long-term renewable power purchase agreements (PPAs) and other open-access structures are emerging as increasingly important alternatives to traditional retail supply. Corporate renewable procurement is already mainstream, and technology companies are becoming more active participants.  
But the optimal strategy varies significantly by location. Open-access charges, renewable availability, grid infrastructure and state regulation can all change the economics of a project. 
Which procurement structures offer the greatest potential for large loads? Where are renewable PPAs most attractive? And how could round-the-clock clean power solutions evolve as demand grows? 
Fill in the form on this page to access our detailed comparison of power procurement options across India’s major data centre hubs. 
Where are the risks and opportunities? 
India’s opportunity is significant, but it is not uniform. 
Data centre development remains concentrated in a handful of strategic hubs, while the next wave of greenfield investment is opening opportunities in emerging markets. 
Policy support is helping to attract investment, but operators must also navigate differences in power availability, renewable access and local infrastructure. 
And electricity is not the only resource under pressure. Water availability is becoming an increasingly important site-selection consideration as AI workloads increase cooling requirements, while regulation remains relatively underdeveloped.  
For data centre operators and other large-load consumers, understanding these differences will be critical to making the right long-term investment decisions.
